processing: Defined by how the tree is managed: side buds and leaves are stripped so only the shoots at the branch tips grow, giving long vine-like branches. The leaf is then usually made as ordinary sun-dried sheng maocha, loose or pressed.
harvest_season: About three to four pickings a year: first spring, second-flush summer tea, autumn and occasionally winter. As with other sheng, spring is the picking people usually pay most for.
appearance_dry: Typical of large-leaf sheng maocha: long, dark green to silvery twisted leaf with visible buds.
appearance_liquor: A clear golden yellow when young, as with other young sheng.
appearance_wet: As with other large-leaf sheng, thick supple olive-green leaves.
taste_profile: Described as mild and sweet, with a smooth floral character, a slightly woody aroma and a lingering finish that lasts through several steeps.

brewing.notes: General young sheng advice: quick rinse, short early steeps, and lengthen slowly so the sweetness comes through before any bitterness.

vintage_note: Sold like other sheng, by harvest year and usually by village or mountain, as loose maocha or pressed cakes; young spring lots are the most common. Since the term describes tree management, ask where the tea grew and look at photos of the trees. No age range is specific to this tea.
description:
Tengtiao means rattan or vine, and the name describes the tree rather than the region. These are Yunnan tea trees trained into long, bare, whip-like branches with leaf gathered at the tips, and tea made from them is sold as a type of its own within pu-erh.

The look comes from a pruning habit, written as 留顶养标: farmers strip the side buds and leaves and leave only the tip shoots to grow. The branches lengthen, side branches stay few and growth is slow. Pickings are spaced out, around three or four a year.

In the cup it is described as gentle: sweet and floral, a little woody, with a long finish and good staying power. Brew it as you would other young sheng, with short early steeps.

It is linked with a scattering of places rather than one: Xiaojinggu in Jinggu County, Taihe in Zhenyuan, Mengku, the eastern half-mountain of Menghai, Xigui in Bangdong, and Yongde. Taste will follow the place as much as the pruning, so the word tengtiao alone tells you little about what is in the bag. Ask for the village and year.
history: The method is attributed to generations of Yunnan farmers, but little is documented about when or where it began, and no dated account is well established. Today the term appears mainly in tea trade writing and on village-labelled sheng, such as old-tree cakes from Banuo in the Mengku area.
